procedural_history.originating_court: VIII Additional District and Sessions Judge, Bengaluru Rural District, Bengaluru
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final Judgment and Order dated 03.02.2016 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Criminal Petition No.5330/2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru allowed Criminal Petition No. 5330/2015 and quashed the criminal proceedings in S.C.No. 219/2013 pending before the VIII Additional District and Sessions Judge, Bengaluru Rural District, Bengaluru. The High Court reasoned that the investigation was illegal and vitiated because it was not steered by a Special Officer appointed by Section 13 of the Act, and allowing the proceedings to continue would be an abuse of the process of the Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court granted leave, heard the parties, allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the trial court to proceed with the matter in accordance with the law. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in interfering with the investigation because an order of the Special Judge was obtained, and the investigation did not suffer from a want of jurisdiction.

directions: Direct the trial court to proceed with the matter in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing criminal proceedings on the ground that the investigation was conducted by an officer not authorized under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956.

facts: The High Court had quashed criminal proceedings against the respondent, which were initiated under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956.
The sole ground for the High Court's decision was that the investigation was conducted by a police officer who was not authorized to do so under the provisions of the Act.
law: The Supreme Court relied on the well-settled legal principle that an illegality or irregularity in an investigation does not automatically vitiate the entire trial.
The function of an investigation is to collect evidence, and a defect in that process does not affect the jurisdiction of the court to conduct the trial.
For a trial to be quashed due to a defective investigation, the accused must demonstrate that the defect has caused them actual prejudice or has resulted in a miscarriage of justice.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred by quashing the proceedings merely on the ground that the investigation was invalid.
The High Court failed to consider the crucial element of whether the unauthorized investigation had caused any prejudice to the accused.
The respondent had not made a case or shown that a miscarriage of justice had occurred as a result of the investigation being conducted by an unauthorized officer.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in quashing the criminal proceedings. A defect in the investigation, without a showing of prejudice to the accused, is not a sufficient ground to terminate a trial. The Court, therefore, set aside the High Court's order and directed the trial court to proceed with the case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing criminal proceedings on the ground that the investigation was conducted by an officer not authorized under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956.
appellant_arguments: There was no infirmity in the investigation.
respondent_arguments: The criminal proceedings should be quashed because the investigation was conducted by an officer not authorized under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An investigation conducted by an officer not authorized by law is a curable illegality and does not, by itself, vitiate the trial unless prejudice to the accused is shown. When such a defect is brought to the court's attention at an early stage, the court must not quash the proceedings but should take necessary steps to cure the defect, such as ordering a reinvestigation by a proper officer.
obiter: The granting of permission by a Magistrate for an investigation by a lower-rank officer is not a routine matter but an exercise of judicial discretion, considering the policy underlying the requirement.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was not justified in quashing criminal proceedings solely on the ground that the investigation was conducted by an unauthorized officer. It is well-settled law that an illegality or irregularity in the investigation does not, by itself, vitiate the trial unless the accused can demonstrate that a miscarriage of justice or prejudice has been caused as a result. The High Court erred by quashing the proceedings without considering the question of prejudice.
legal_tests_applied: An illegality committed in the course of investigation does not affect the competence and jurisdiction of the court for trial, and the invalidity of the preceding investigation does not vitiate the result unless a miscarriage of justice has been caused thereby.

When a breach of a mandatory provision relating to investigation is brought to the court's notice at an early stage of the trial, the court must consider the nature and extent of the violation and pass appropriate orders for such reinvestigation as may be called for, rather than automatically quashing the proceedings.
policy_considerations: The function of investigation is merely to collect evidence, and any irregularity or even illegality in the course of collecting evidence can scarcely be considered by itself to affect the legality of the trial by an otherwise competent court.

To ignore a breach of a peremptory provision regarding investigation when brought to the court's notice early would be to virtually make a dead letter of a provision enacted on grounds of public policy for the benefit of the accused.

When such a breach is identified early, it would not be fair to the accused to force them to wait until the conclusion of the trial to show prejudice; the court should instead obviate the prejudice by ordering appropriate reinvestigation at that stage.
